utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-69-T, the Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Knoops, are you ready to continue your cross-examination? Mr. Tihic, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you'd given yesterday, that you'd speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness. Mr. Witness, I would like to finish some questions which I left yesterday with respect to the position of the Crisis Staff. Now, in your statement of 1995 - that's P174 - on page 3, you have stated that you once asked Mr. Blagoje Simic why he wanted a war, as one of his sons could be killed. Can you remember asking him that? And Mr. Simic's answer was that he was prepared to sacrifice all three of his children for war, and you stated that he would change his eyes -- his eyes would change, and he would look like mad man when he spoke like that. Do you remember saying that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember it roughly the way you quoted it, and he looked more and more like Milosevic, in terms of his conduct and behaviour, and also his unwillingness to settle in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: If, please, Exhibit 1747 could be pulled up, Prosecution Exhibit 1747; 65 ter, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, before you, you see a document which is signed on the 15th May, 1992. Are you familiar with the signature of the author of this document?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't see the signature here yet, not on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Is it possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could we move the picture in such a way that we see a signature, if there's a -- yes, there we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, you see the signature of the author?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: You agree this is a document signed by Mr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is his signature. I've forgotten a bit what his signature looks like, but it was something like that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If Mr. Knoops could please switch off his microphone when he's not using it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, do you agree that if you look at the top of this document, it's issued by the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac; you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the date is the 15th of May. By then, I was already in Batajnica, in the camp in Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, sir. Well, according to this document, on the 15th of May, 1992, the Crisis Staff, i.e., Mr. Simic, requested for combat use of aviation and armoured mechanised equipment?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And can you see to whom this request was addressed?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to the prime minister personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So you agree with me that this document actually shows that Mr. Simic, on behalf of the Crisis Staff, requested military support? You agree with that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Now, would you agree with me that the Crisis Staff was, in those days, empowered to direct and co-ordinate or at least request for military support?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had the right to ask for military assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Do you agree that the Crisis Staff had the responsibility for directing and co-ordinating the work of the police in Bosanski Samac, including also the work of the TOs?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that's the way it was, roughly, as far as the local police was concerned and the local Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes. Would you agree, Mr. Tihic, that under Yugoslavian law at that time the TO units and staff came under the JNA in times of emergency and war and were subsumed under a unified system of command of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, could you please, before you ask a rather legal question, explain exactly what you understand, in terms of time, what you understand to be Yugoslavian law, apart from -- I do not know, of course, the witness is a trained lawyer, although he did not appear as an expert, but mid-May, in a situation which is described as Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, at least the witness should know exactly what he should orient upon, in terms of what kind of law was applicable at the time. Because you're talking about the JNA, was the JNA still the armed force of this state? It raises a huge number of questions which I would like you to go through one by one, rather than to ask the witness a short question which he might answer, but leave the Chamber in doubt as to what exactly the gist of his answer -- what the basis for his answer is. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, in general, in times of war or emergency, a state of emergency, the JNA conducting combat operations in a certain area, is it, as far as you know, the case that in such a scenario the TO units and staff commandeered the command of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the Territorial Defence units of Republika Srpska were illegal, you see. There was only the Staff of the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not of Republika Srpska. So that institution was not legal. Also, what was illegal was the presence of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina after the European Union recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 6th of April. Now, to discuss who could issue orders to who amongst them, well, they're all illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, with all due respect, my question is not about issuing orders. My question is simply: Do you know whether, in times of war or emergency, the TO units come under command of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, if you are under the command of someone, the commander can give orders. Would you agree with that? Yes. So to say it's not about who's giving orders to whom, that is an implicit element of command. Therefore, you are invited to rephrase your question and questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes. May I please pull up Defence document 2D00044, page 12608.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: 2D00044. It's a 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We'd just like to state that we were, to my knowledge, not notified of the documents that the Stanisic Defence was going to be putting to the witness. So we were informed -- if I'm not mistaken, I believe we were informed that some of the Seselj documents -- evidence was going to be put to him, but we -- so far for 1747 and for this document now, to the best our knowledge, we were not informed that they were going to be put to him. So we're not objecting to them -- to their use. We're just asking for the Defence, please, to let us know in advance what documents they're going to use. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Apologies, if that's not being correctly done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, there's no objection against using them at this moment, at least, I take it, as far as you know until now.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Thus far, no objections, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, I'll ask you to look at line 15 'til 19.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not in the Bosnian language here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: If it's a non-translation, I will read it out to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Usually, it's not the task of our interpreters, although they now and then greatly assist us to translate written documents. However, it happens now and then that we have a small portion of a document which you would then read. So, therefore, if you leave it to a very small portion, and if you would be so kind next time to perhaps submit, even on an urgent basis, any written text which you'd like to put to a witness in his own language, where the original is in another language. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the specific portion I'm referring to reads: "Q. All right. Fine. Now, you know that in case the JNA conducted operations in a certain area, that all the units of the Territorial Defence came under the command of the JNA, and that was according to the concept of then total national or All People's Defence? "A. Yes, that's logical, when it comes to an external enemy, an external foe."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA operates in case of an external enemy, not internal conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on. Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we just -- I'm trying to -- I can't see which page this is. Could it be scrolled up so that I have the page number. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, in your statement, P173, page 6, you stated, in 1994, that some of the Muslim members of the 4th Detachment called you to ask you to call the JNA and ask for help, since Arkan and Seselj's men were already killing people in the town. Can you remember making that statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not state that these were members of the 4th Detachment, but members of my party. It must be a mistake. They called me, and they asked me to talk, to have members of the JNA come and prevent these killings. That was the kind of information that was there. However, I could not make any contact then. I was not able to communicate. And it is a fact that by then the JNA was already in town with this combat vehicle. That's why I received that call. And I know that by my neighbour's house this vehicle went by with a long gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I put it to you that it was the local community that called in the JNA. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot agree, because I don't know. I don't think that was the case. I was part of the local community, too. I should know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Were you part of the Crisis Staff, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and also within the political party. I was on the Commission for Protection and Security. So within the local community, there was a forum where we used to meet. It wasn't called the Crisis Staff. It was a body consisting of representatives of all parties, and then there was the representative of the 4th Detachment, that is to say, Mr. Simic, on behalf of the SDS -- on behalf of the SDS, Filip Pajevic [phoen], then Simo Zaric, on behalf of the 4th Detachment, and then -- or, rather --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, sorry to interrupt you. Would you please be disciplined in answering the questions. Please answer my questions as short as possible because of the time, sir. If we ask you to elaborate on an answer, I will ask you. So would you please confine to my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, one of your previous answer -- questions and one of the documents you've shown to the witness was the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If a couple of lines later you just refer to the Crisis Staff, then the witness says, Yes, but... and then he starts thinking about that it wasn't the real Crisis Staff. It's partly due to the way you put the question to the witness. The first question was, Was there a Crisis Staff before the Crisis Staff we just referred to, that is, the Crisis Staff of the Municipality of Bosanski Samac, of the Serbian Republic of ... then we have a clearly-defined Crisis Staff. If you want to ask about any other Crisis Staff, unless you'd want to ask him whether he was a member of the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that what you had in mind, because he was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: I believe you're speaking about the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But apparently in terms of time, there has been a Crisis Staff of which you just asked the witness about, and now you're asking him about a Crisis Staff -- I take it, then, a different one, or?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: I will rephrase my question, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, were you a member of the Crisis Staff of Bosanski Samac we referred to yesterday, of which Mr. Simic was the president?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the attack on Bosanski Samac took place on the 17th April, 1992. You stated that seven days before, the Government of Belgrade was not aware of what was going on in Bosanski Samac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not mention the government from Belgrade, and I have no idea how familiar they were with the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: If document P174 could be pulled up, please, page 4 of the English version. It's the second-last paragraph of page 4 of the English version, and the bottom of page 5 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: You have it before you, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please tell me which part? The one-but-last paragraph, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Starting with: "On 10th April, 1992, I saw Maslic at a meeting commemorating the liberation of Bosanski Samac after the Second World War." And I especially ask you to pay attention to the last sentence: "He replied that even people in the Presidency in Belgrade didn't know who was doing what."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the celebration of the liberation of Bosanski Samac after the Second World War. It was a big event. I walked up to Andjelko and said hello to him, and this is the reply I got from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So he actually told you that within the Presidency in Belgrade, nobody knew what was going on or who was doing what; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you. I move on to the next topic, and that relates to the support you mentioned yesterday. I have before me the draft transcripts. Yesterday, you testified, on page 27 of the draft transcripts, line 14: "They would never have been able to do that --" Sorry: "They would never have been able to do this had they not had Belgrade support." My question is: Who do you refer to with the words "they"? "They would never have been able to do that without Belgrade support."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have in mind those who attacked Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: And what do you refer to with the words "Belgrade support"?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Belgrade support. I can guess that it was the support from the JNA and the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia. Such support could not have arrived from Sarajevo. It must have originated in Belgrade. How else could they have been given weapons, and who else could have been -- could have ordered the special forces to come in? These orders must have come from Belgrade. Who gave the arms to the Serb Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So you are guessing. Have you any basis for your guess, other than maybe a book you've read?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is crystal clear that if weapons are being distributed and if helicopters were there bringing in special forces, it must have arrived on some orders. Blagoje Simic could not have ordered that a helicopter should arrive and weapons be distributed. It could have only been done by the General Staff of the JNA or the Serbian Ministry of the Interior, no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any idea how much weapons were distributed in those days in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of those several months, you should say, because the JNA was distributing weapons for a period of time. More or less each and every Serbian person received a piece of weapons, and they were simply issued with weapons free of charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: I put to you that according to facts and figures in those months, as you mentioned, approximately 60.000 guns were distributed in Bosnia; whereby the SDP, distributed only itself more than 70.000 weapons. Would you agree with me that considering these amounts of weapons, that this could have only been distributed by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, according to facts and figures, you said approximately 60.000 guns were distributed in Bosnia; whereas, by the SDP, already 70.000. I have some difficulties in including 70.000 in 60.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honours, 17, 17, 1-7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, 17.000 weapons. Could we hear of your source, Mr. Knoops?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: You'll find that, Your Honours, on page 77 of the pre-trial Defence brief, whereby the sources are mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Page 77, where also the documentation on which the Defence relies is mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you agree that these amounts of weapons could only be distributed by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, could you clarify for me what you meant by "the SDP"? It's an acronym for what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: The Socialist Democratic Party. It could be the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the SDS is a different matter, although I don't know of such data. I think that the weapons came from the JNA. As for what the figures were, that is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: That's fair enough, Mr. Witness. Would you agree with me that, actually, in the time-frame of April and the month thereafter, all assistance whatsoever, in terms of finances, fuel, weapons, everything logistically thinkable was delivered by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that my learned friend has established a basis for the witness's knowledge of the answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please establish such knowledge, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you have any direct knowledge on the source of the logistical assistance, apart from the weapons you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any direct knowledge. As regards the distribution of weapons to the 4th Detachment in Bosanski Samac, I know, though, that the JNA gave them weapons. There may have been between 3 and 400 pieces. That's what I know directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, that's fair enough. Mr. Witness, do you know whether, apart from the JNA, the channeling of weapons also went through the intelligence services within the military, i.e., the JNA?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: On several occasions in your statements, you have mentioned the name of Mr. Petrovic of KOS. Now, I've noticed that the KOS was involved in helping the 4th Detachment and was also present when you were brought to a detention camp. Do you have any knowledge whether the KOS was involved with the paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic was in the Brcko JNA Garrison. He had contacts with the 4th Detachment, which, in turn, was part of the military structure. I did see him there on one occasion when I was detained in Brcko. He introduced himself to me as the chief of KOS in that particular garrison. As for his contacts with any paramilitary formations, that is something I don't know about. I do know that he had contacts with the 4th Detachment and that he came to ourselves a number of times with Zoran Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, can you confirm that the military police was working with the paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't. I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: You can confirm, though, because it's in your statement, that the military police was involved in the beatings of prisoners; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in Brcko, not the military police. They even prevented one of the Red Berets from doing so. They drove him out of the building. We were there hit by other soldiers, but not the MPs. In Mitrovica and in Batajnica, that, yes, perhaps. We were escorted by military policemen from Mitrovica to Batajnica, and the military policeman escorting us did hit me twice on the head with his baton, but that was all. Later on, we were handed over to the regular JNA forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So you, therefore, can confirm that the JNA military police was involved in certain locations with beating prisoners?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They transferred us from Batajnica to Mitrovica, and on that occasion, I received two blows. And as we were being thrown out of the Pinzgauers, perhaps they hit us once or twice again. Then they handed us over to those in charge of the Sremska Mitrovica prison, and the mistreatment continued but there were no more MPs around. Those who beat us there were plain soldiers, I think, not military policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I put to you that Dragoljub Djordjevic, alias Crni, was under the command of the 7th Tactical Group, the commander of the group, the then-Colonel Stefan Nikolic of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. He was outside that chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: In the Seselj case, you testified that the JNA actually controlled the paramilitary units. Can you remember giving that statement?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I don't remember having said that in those words. To me, even the TO Staff of Republika Srpska was paramilitary because it was illegal. The JNA did provide support, though, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Could we, again, please pull up Defence document 2D00045, transcripts in the Seselj case, 4th December, 2008, page 12679, especially line 16 to 18. Considering the absence of a B/C/S translation, if Your Honours allow me, I will just read out these three lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Witness, the question is put to you there: "Do you know that some units of the JNA also wore red berets?" That was the question put to you. Your answer on the 4th of December, 2008, is: "I don't know, but they came as part of the JNA, as part of the army. Whether they were formally under the control of the JNA or the police, that's something I don't know."

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this is not the way you originally put the question. I know that they did not agree with Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolic and that there were issues. I could see that myself. And this is what Simo Zaric said, as well as others, that they were not respecting the law, and they were in no one's control. That's why Nikolic sent his unit. They were beating us and mistreating us. Had there been any co-ordination, that would not have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Marcus.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir. Learned counsel is taking this out of context, which, normally, of course, he has the right to put which ever part he wants to the witness; but in light of the fact that the witness does not have the full translation of the question and answer which preceded this question and answer, it seems to me to be rather misleading, in terms of the witness's prior evidence, respectfully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first check that. I'm just checking the context and the way in which the question was phrased. Mr. Knoops, on page 15, line 18, you said that the witness testified that the JNA actually controlled the paramilitary units. Then you referred to a portion of the transcript which reads: "Do you know that some units of the JNA also wore red berets?" And this was in the context of a discussion on who was who in certain activities. I think the witness correctly said that what you put to him is not the same as what was covered by your first question. First of all, your question was far wider, and, second, the witness apparently testified in the context of a specific discussion not about paramilitaries, but about units of the JNA who wore red berets, and he didn't say anything about the command of paramilitaries. He said what he said, and that is that some units of the JNA, apparently wearing red berets, came with the JNA as part of the army, and whether they were formally under the control of the JNA, that's something he doesn't know. So, therefore, a rather -- certainly not what you've put to him in your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Could I rephrase the question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Witness, the words "they," mentioned in this answer, "but they came as part of the JNA," to whom are you referring to with "they"?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure who I had in mind out of everyone included. I know those who were there, Djordjevic and the rest, who were not under Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolic's control. He couldn't issue orders to them. They were a separate force. Simo Zaric was, however, under Nikolic's control, as a part of the 4th Detachment. As to the extent of Djordjevic's and Nikolic's co-operation, and the manner of that co-operation, that is something I'm not familiar with. I only know that they disagreed on many things. That's why Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolic sent his unit to take us out of the Samac camp to Brcko. He disagreed with the methods they used and the beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Could we please go to Defence document 2D00044, the testimony of Mr. Tihic in Seselj, 3rd December, page 12548.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you put any question, I'd like to read the relevant portion. Could we -- it is 12548. Which lines, Mr. Knoops, you would like to ask questions about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: In line 17, Your Honour, 'til 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, the question is put to you there that: "If the Red Berets did come with a helicopter from the JNA, this seems to demonstrate that the army does control these units. What can you say about this?" Your answer is: "Yes, of course. The army controlled all those paramilitary units." What do you mean with the words "all those paramilitary units"?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honours. Please, the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we then read the whole of the answer? Let me slowly read your answer in its entirety, Mr. Tihic. When Judge Antonetti asked you what you could tell about the army controlling a unit, "Red Berets ... come with a helicopter," you said the following: "Yes, of course. The army controlled all those paramilitary units. Those were not paramilitary units; they were special units either of MUP of Serbia or of the JNA. They maybe were not officially labelled as such, but nobody else could have arrived on a JNA helicopter and have so much weapons. So these were special units operating pursuant to orders of either the police, the military, or security services; and they wore military uniforms with some other insignia other than that of the JNA." That was your answer to the question. Mr. Knoops, if you, please, ask the witness what you intended to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, did you give this statement after -- or the testimony after reading the book of Simo Zaric which you mentioned yesterday?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I read Simo Zaric's book only a fortnight ago, and this was much earlier, perhaps two years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes. But you agree that the book of Simo Zaric is from before your testimony in the case of Mr. Seselj; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, but I didn't read it then. I read it perhaps 10 to 15 days ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you have testified yesterday about the special forces from Serbia. Could you please give us a definition of your understanding of those special forces?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My definition would be that these were skilled and trained members of the armed forces, with a certain amount of war experience and war skills. You could clearly see that difference when compared to those local forces of ours who picked up their weapons for the first time and who were not familiar with the whole thing. These people behaved differently, moved about differently, they spoke differently. You could see that these were special forces who could wage war, who knew how to shoot, and who had no difficulty killing. That's why they were special forces, as opposed to those who were, in a certain way, mobilised and who took up weapons for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Well, did they ever introduce them to you, yourself, as special forces from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you how they introduced themselves. I think I mentioned that yesterday; Arkan's men, Tigers with those four Ss. And I could only see their insignia when they showed it to me. They didn't come especially to introduce themselves to me. But when they interrogated me and beat me, they showed me their insignia, and I saw that these were Arkan's Tigers. And the TO Staff, I was shown other insignia; I saw some other insignia as well, but these are the ones I remember, because I saw them when I dared look. On occasion, I would raise my head, trying to see around me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: But, Mr. Tihic, is it correct that nobody of those groups you mentioned ever told you that they were special forces from Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not introduce themselves as such, but you could tell that from their conduct, from their speech, and from what Djokic told me. He told me who they were when they arrived in that helicopter. I knew they were from Serbia, and that is not something that can be disputed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, is it correct that the name "Special Forces Serbia" was actually a name given by the local population to them? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the camp, we called them "specijalci," "special forces." Before the camp, people from Batkusa and from my party, told me that these were special forces who had come from Serbia in a helicopter. And they also said that they were Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So it is correct that the local people named them "Special Forces;" is that true, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the local people named them. We called them "Specials."

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: In your statement -- please pull up P173, page 13. It's the third paragraph from the bottom. I'm not sure whether -- starting with -- no, it was, sorry: "Grga Zubak was already unconscious ..." Page 13. Mr. Witness, you see your statement before you, starting with: "Grga Zubak was already unconscious ..." And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see two pages 13 at this moment, both in English. Could we wait until we have found the relevant page in B/C/S so that the witness is able to read with us. And I think we have it -- yes. It's the semi-last paragraph on your screen at this moment, Mr. Tihic. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, you see the sentence starting: "During our stay, members of the Red Berets, who were Arkan soldiers, were threatening us"?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an awkward expression, but I told you there was that one with a red beret who came to the prison and threatened that he would slaughter us, kill us, but the police removed him. I know that, and I've already told you that several times. And I also saw those in the courtyards through a small window. I saw similar people, Specials, as we called them, who stood out from the rest of them who wore olive-drab uniforms. That's why I thought they were Arkan's men or something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, my question is simply: Is it correct that the -- that Arkan's soldiers were mentioned by the local population as "Red Berets"?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan's men is one thing. Red Berets is another thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, looking at the clock, I'm trying to finish on that before the session is over. Yesterday, you testified about the probability that there was some kind of a co-ordination between the separate groups. You remember, Mr. Witness, that in the Seselj case, you gave a statement or, actually, a summary of all your statements, in which you -- and that is our Defence document --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I put it already to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know what you want to put to the witness, apparently a statement of him?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: If it would assist counsel, I can give you the ERN in English and in B/C/S, if you're talking about Mr. Tihic's Seselj 92 ter statement in the Seselj case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Okay. It's 0635-0160 to 0635-0181. It has the same ERN for English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: I'm grateful for the assistance, Ms. Marcus. Page 12, paragraph 38, last sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, this document has been made available to the Chamber because apparently there once has been a thought of tendering it as a 92 ter document. Now, unfortunately, the page after page 11 states "Page ID 91576." That page could not be found, or "file type not supported." Therefore, we -- and therefore we are missing page 12, and we are also missing, therefore, paragraph 38. Is there any way in which we -- do we have the same in the -- under the same 65 ter number? If you could assist, please, Ms. Marcus, to provide us with the 65 ter number under which it was up-loaded. We can even see that from -- let me have a look. It was on one of your previous lists; not on the last one anymore. If you could give us the 65 ter number, then we can look at it on our screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Just a moment, Your Honours. We're checking that. Your Honours, I'm sorry, we don't seem to have a 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it has been found by Madam Registrar on the basis of its ERN number. Paragraph 38 apparently starts at the previous page. I don't know what portion you would like the witness to look at, Mr. Knoops. If it's the beginning, we have to go down one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it's actually the last sentence of page -- of paragraph 38.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: The very last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please read the last portion of paragraph 38. It's the paragraph preceding paragraph 39.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have read it. Yes, I've read it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, do you agree that speaking about the Grey Wolves, of which you say some were Red Berets, some were Chetniks with long beards, some JNA soldiers, you have no idea in what way the co-ordination was done and who had to obey whose orders?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, if possible, for the sake of the completeness of the record, perhaps the paragraph could be read into the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you like the whole of the paragraph to be read into the record?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: The part that the learned counsel directed the witness to read before answering the question, Your Honour, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think he -- well, he did not literally quote from it, but -- I think it's important to read it, Mr. Knoops, because what paragraph 38 says is: "I noticed many different soldiers there. Some were Grey Wolves, some were Red Berets, and some were Chetniks with long beards. Also some JNA soldiers were there. They had operated together in the attack on Bosanski Samac." And then: "Firstly, members of the Serbian Territorial Defence and the paramilitary units attacked. The JNA joined in later, around 11.00. In what way the co-ordination was done and who had to obey whose orders, I cannot say, but they were all together there." That gives the full context. Please put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, is this, indeed, your position? Could you please answer the question with yes or no .

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, what is your understanding of Red Berets? Could you give us a definition of "Red Berets"?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I perceived and experienced all of them as enemies who were there -- who were simply there, who looked dangerous, who looked intimidating. Some sported beards. They were full of hatred, and it looked to me as if I had returned to the Second World War, to some movies about partisans, and I could almost see all of them epitomised there. The Red Berets were nothing special, the Grey Wolves, Arkan's men; they were all one and the same enemies, full of hatred, hostility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, my final question is the following: You never, before 2008, in any statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecution or in any of the trials you testified, you never mentioned anything about the Ministry of Interior Affairs, yet yesterday in your statement before this Court - it's draft transcript page 52 - you suggested or assumed that -- asking to whom those special forces were answerable, you said: "The Ministry of Interior of Serbia or something like that, state security. I don't know. I cannot say." I put to you that since you never testified about the Ministry of Interior Affairs before, that your testimony before this Court was simply here to suggest that the Ministry of Interior was involved, and that that suggestion was based on sources which were made available to you by third persons and books, like the book you mentioned yesterday. And I suggest that you don't have any direct knowledge and you're just speculating about who potentially would have directed those special forces. What is your answer to this, sir?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I'm trying to tell you all I know. I've not heard a question like that on any of the previous occasions. This is the first time somebody's asking me, and I'm just giving you my assumption. I didn't -- never said, expressly, that they received orders from the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia or some other Defence ministry. I only assumed that that's where they could receive their orders from. I did not hear questions of that kind before, but let me assure you that I will never say and speak about anything that I did not either experience, personally, and/or came to a conclusion, personally. I can only tell the truth. Sometimes I can't be very concise in my answers because sometimes, although you may ask me to answer with either yes or no, it's impossible. You know, there are a lot of shades between black and white, there are a lot of shades of grey in between.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Witness, we can conclude, therefore, that you do not know -- you have no knowledge on the whereabouts of the special forces you mentioned, whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Objection. Unclear question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please rephrase, Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: You have no direct knowledge on the special forces you mentioned in your testimony; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, objection again. It's still not a very clear question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do agree with you, Ms. Marcus. Mr. Knoops, please -- are you talking about existence as a unit, or could you please be precise, because the witness explained what he understood to be special forces, though that knowledge he has, but that appears not to be -- he appears not to be -- well, not to talk in terms which you do understand or which are in line with your understanding. And, therefore, if you'd please put the question in such a way that the answer can assist the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, you don't know -- have knowledge on the answer to the question by whom these special forces were directed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you what I know, and I told you about my assumptions, who they were answerable to, who they were not answerable to, and I can only repeat the same words again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Knoops. We'll first have a break. Could the witness already be excused. We'll have a break of half an hour or approximately. We'd like to see you back after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Knoops, I several times noticed that if you summarise or refer to a part of a statement, that sometimes precision is lacking at a level, which could create confusion. Let me just give you one example. Page 24, line 18, of today's transcript, you said: "Mr. Witness, do you agree that speaking about the Grey Wolves, of which you say some were Red Berets, some were Chetniks with long beards, some JNA soldiers, you have no idea in what way the co-ordination was done and who had to obey whose orders?" Now, if you look at the line of the statement, the witness is talking about soldiers of several kinds. Some were Grey Wolves, some were Red Berets. So you misrepresented what the witness said there, because in your phrase "Red Berets," "Chetniks," and "JNA soldiers" were -- or at least the Red Berets were Grey Wolves, and that's not what that line says. And it's not the first time. I also would like to invite you to, if you ask the witness to agree with you on a certain matter, to split it up, not to tell him the full story of Cinderella and then ask whether he agrees or not. It could be that he agrees that Cinderella is called by that name or that part of what happened in that story is true or not. Please split that up clearly so that we know what the witness agrees with and what the witness does not agree with, that that is clear, and that it's not a kind of a all-in bargain to accept or not to accept. Could you please keep that in mind. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 10 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic or Mr. Bakrac. Who is it? Yes, but Mr. Knoops has another matter. Mr. Knoops.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm sorry to interrupt, but we would like to tender the first document I presented today, Rule 65 ter 1747, as -- Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was the letter or was it the --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: It was the letter from the Crisis Staff to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, seeking for support, military support.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will not object to the tendering. I just wanted to say that it seems to us that the witness didn't authenticate that document. However, we have no objections as to relevance or reliability or authenticity. So if the Defence is seeking to tender it from the Bar table, we would have no objection to that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As well, of course, the document was introduced to the witness, but all the questions in relation to this document asked to the witness, I could have answered them myself. Of course, the witness could have known something, but whether it came from here, whether it went to there, whether it dealt with this subject, apparently the witness had no knowledge about it, and therefore bar tabling the document would be perhaps the most appropriate way of dealing with it, because I think there were six or seven questions, and all of them I had no difficulty at all to answer them, in a position not to have any further knowledge than the letter and its content. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit D16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Petrovic, will it be you who will cross-examine Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, you'll be cross-examined by Mr. Petrovic. Mr. Petrovic is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Tihic, I have a few questions for you in relation to your overall testimony. I'd like to start with something that you said in your statement from 1994. P173 is the number of that document. You say that Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolic organised small groups of armed men, that he distributed weapons, that these groups were deployed in villages around Samac. Do you remember having said that? I would like to hear whether you know why it was that Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolic did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. If you refer to the statement, would you always refer to page or paragraph number so that we are able to verify whether the reference to the statement is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, to add to that, it seems to be a compound question, first asking, Do you remember, but there's no answer from the witness, and then the second question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is P173, page 3 in B/C/S. This is how it starts: "Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolic was commander of the 17th Tactical Group." That is what it says at the beginning of that paragraph. It is page 2 in English, the one-but-last paragraph. It says: "... Nikolic was commander of the 17th Tactical Group which covered the Posavina region. The 4th Detachment was a part of this group ..." And so on and so forth. "Nikolic organised small groups in different towns. He gave weapons to the Serbian civilians in different towns, but he was actually the deputy commander of the JNA in Brcko, and one part of this unit was displaced into villages around Bosanski Samac."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, does this reflect your statement, what I read out just now?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question to you is whether you have an explanation as to why Nikolic did that, what you described here in your statement.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the 4th Detachment was established for the town of Bosanski Samac, we were then told, and it was Lieutenant-Colonel Nikolic who said that, or Simo Zaric, that they were doing that, that they were establishing detachments and distributing weapons in order to prevent inter-ethnic conflicts, especially as far as Samac is concerned, because it was on the border with Croatia, so then that detachment would prevent the possible entry of groups or individuals from Croatia. He mentioned HOS members, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: From today's vantage point, do you think that it was Nikolic who was preparing an attack on Samac and the other towns in the region?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From today's point of view and on the basis of the knowledge and information that I have, I don't think that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in the area that we are talking about, the area of Posavina, what was the strongest force there, who had the best equipment, who had the most manpower, who controlled the area in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The strongest force was the JNA, by far, and then the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, if I could take you back to your previous question, you asked whether, from today's point of view and on the basis of the knowledge and information that, I take it, you have -- no, he said, I have -- no, you asked the witness: "Do you think, from today's vantage point, it was Nikolic who was preparing an attack." That question asks for a judgement rather than for a fact. That's one. And, second, refers to "today's vantage point." For the Chamber, totally unknown what would be included in this judgement or what would not be included. So I would like to emphasise, again, let's try to ask witnesses of fact about facts and try to refrain from directly asking for a judgement, an opinion. Not to say that it won't slip in now and then and that sometimes it will be a bit mixed. But as soon as any portion of judgement or opinion slips in, it should be perfectly clear what the factual basis of such, of that part of the testimony is. And to be quite honest, it's totally unclear to me in relation to your last question -- your semi-last question. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same document, that is to say, P173, page 4, page 4. I'll tell you what page in the English version. Page 3 -- at the very beginning of page 4 in English, rather. The very beginning of page 4. I'm referring to that sentence: "At some meetings, I tried to convince Simo Zaric to organise the Territorial Defence, and it seemed to me that Zaric wanted to give up organising the 4th Detachment. However, he was pressured by Nikolic and the JNA."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Tihic, to the best of your knowledge, what kind of pressure was this that Zaric did not manage to resist? What was that all about?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At meetings, I proposed that this 4th Detachment that was within the JNA be incorporated in the Territorial Defence of the town of Bosanski Samac, of the municipality of Bosanski Samac. Simo Zaric could not accept that. He claimed that the question of the 4th Detachment was within the authority of the JNA, that he was not entitled to pass that kind of decision. The JNA was his command -- its commander, and Nikolic was the commander, specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So Zaric acted in accordance with what JNA orders said; right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And Zaric could not oppose what came from the appropriate JNA command?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was part of those structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On page 5 of the same document, you mention the arrival of the Red Berets by helicopter. I'll give you the exact reference in a second. Page 5 in B/C/S, the last paragraph. It is page 5 in English, the first paragraph. I would be interested in the following. We know how you came about this piece of information, but I would like to ask you the following: Is it correct that you do not have any direct knowledge as to who was in that helicopter that your client mentions in this situation?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any direct knowledge, except for what I heard from my client.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that you do not know whether there were people from Samac in that helicopter or some other people?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I know is that it was people who had come from Serbia, that they were not from Samac. I was not present as they were disembarking from the helicopter, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you do not know about these people from the helicopter; namely, whether they had gone through any kind of training?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But they were trained, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to go back to your previous reply, when you say that you know that they were not from Samac. I would like to remind you of your testimony in the Seselj case. 2D45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber, nor the witness, has direct access to 65 ter numbers. Would you like to have it on the screen, Mr. -- yes, there we are.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, could it please be called up on the screen, 2D45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And could you give a page number.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 12678 and 12679.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On this first page that I mentioned, at the very bottom of the page, the witness says: [In English] "... whether that included people from Bosanski Samac who had gone to some special training, I don't know." [Interpretation] Is that correct, Mr. Tihic; namely, that the only thing you can say about this is assume this and that, but you don't basically know it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only say what I found out from my client. I've already referred to that. He told me that they were from Serbia, how they behaved in the village and what they did there. I don't know anything more than that, more than what he had said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tihic, what did you think at the time of the war -- what did you think -- which structure, which formation did these persons with the red berets belong to during the war?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, at the first moment when I received this information, I thought that since they had arrived by helicopter, well, for me helicopters are linked to the JNA. However, later, when I was in the camp, I realised that there was a difference between the JNA and these specials, that it was not one and the same thing. That is what I can say. The specials were somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you what you thought during the war. Did they belong to the military or someone else?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one moment, at first, I thought they belonged to the military, but later on I was convinced that they belonged to someone else, that they were attached to another command. When I was in the camp, then I got another impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please call up 2D44. That is the Seselj transcript. Page 12549. That is, line 9: [In English] "They wore military uniforms, so I thought they were part of the military. But after the war, I learned that the Red Berets had been part of the police of Serbia ..." [Interpretation] I understand your statement in the following way: that you heard these stories about who these people belonged to only after the war.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who they exactly belonged to, I found out only after the war. But during the war, I saw - I'm talking about the second part of my knowledge, as it were - that they did not belong to the military. But I didn't know who it was that they belonged to. After the war, I heard who the Red Berets actually belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in the JNA and later on in the Army of Yugoslavia there were special formations that wore red berets by way of headgear? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Have you perhaps heard of the 63rd Air-Borne Brigade from Nis, that they wore red berets, and there is a great deal of indicia that they took part in various territories of the former Yugoslavia that we are discussing?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since we have this page on our screen, page 12549 in the Seselj testimony, Mr. Knoops, could I invite you to read what we see here what the witness says about the MUP, because I might at a later stage remind you that you earlier put something to the witness, that he never had spoken about certain matters. And since it is on the screen, I would like you to read it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: I know, Your Honour. I said before "2008." I know what is in the Seselj transcripts. My question was, to the witness in my own cross-examination, whether he -- whether it is correct that he never mentioned the MUP before 2008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll have a look it -- at the exact way in which the question was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KNOOPS
utterances.text: That was the reference to this portion in the Seselj transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, at page 3122, you said - at least that's what I understood - that the people who had come from outside to Bosanski Samac wanted to destroy the tolerance among the peoples in that area. I may have misunderstood, but it seemed to me that you shift the entire blame onto those who came from outside.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they carry most of the blame. The local Serbs, the local formations were not in favour of what they were doing and the means they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Then please explain the ultimatum that was in place which was given -- issued to you by SDS representatives to the inhabitants of Bosanski Samac. They said, Samac must be Serbian and no one else's. It is clearly an ultimatum. What did it mean, and where did it come from?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was issued by Mr. Blagoje Simic and the SDS. I referred to the crimes they committed, that they beat people and killed people. I said that those who guarded us there condemned that. People were trying to get us out of there. They didn't like Simo Zaric because his wife was Muslim, but he did try to help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please focus on my question. Who issued the ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did tell you already. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is Blagoje Simic a local, or did he come from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a local.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did that ultimatum mean? Could it be imposed without bloodshed?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the way he presented it. First, he tried to have us agree to it, and then he said that they would resort to force. They, indeed, tried. He participated in the attack on Samac. There was no other way; only to use force.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the core and the cause of the conflict was local as well as general in Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is to say, a wish of one structure, without qualifications, to create a state within a state and perhaps annex it to another state?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the local structures could not have done anything without Belgrade's support. They did not have the power to do that; not without that support, in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What I'm asking you, therefore, is the following: Did the conflict arise from the relationships in the field?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The causes of a conflict cannot be limited only to one municipality, to Bosanski Samac, but it was across Bosnia-Herzegovina and beyond in the entire former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, that would be a matter of a long discussion, but we won't do that now. When you were brought to the police station on the 18th of April, in front of the station, as far as I understand, you saw a number of people whom you describe as the Grey Wolves, Arkan's men, Red Berets, members of the JNA. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me this: Out of the number of people and units there - Arkan's men, Seselj's men, the Grey Wolves, Red Berets - at the moment of your arrest, how could you distinguish between them? How could you tell who belonged to whom? How is that possible?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there is a space inside the police station building where I waited for Djordjevic to see me for a while. In that area, there were people with JNA uniforms, people with special forces uniforms, people with or without beards, policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question -- or, rather, almost an assertion, is that: It is impossible to ascertain who belonged to the Grey Wolves, who belonged to Arkan's men, to Seselj's men, or to the Red Berets, for that matter; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I described them as such, because later that day some of those people introduced themselves as Arkan's men, and I simply put all of them on the list based on the knowledge I had when I met Djordjevic and when I was taken for interrogation, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I do not dispute that. But the essence is this: When you saw all those people together, you don't know who was from where?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one of them beat me there, and he was from the special forces. He spoke Ikavian.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: That's another matter I wanted to ask you about. How can you distinguish between the specials from Serbia and others? What makes a special forces member from Serbia different from others in late April 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained a number of times. I can do it again. Their uniforms were camouflage military uniforms. Next, their appearance and behaviour was different. You could tell they were trained. And their speech was Serbian. The second thing: Samac is a small town, and I know almost everyone. I can tell you who comes from what village. If someone came from Serbia, they speak differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I understand well, the basic points of distinction between the two groups were the camouflage uniforms and the Ikavian dialect. Correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You couldn't notice any other distinctions?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the appearance of assertion of power.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the beginning of this topic. You will agree, won't you, that once in front of the station you were no longer able to distinguish who belonged to what unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw people from different units. As for who belonged to what unit, that I can't tell you. But I knew that these were special forces, these were the police, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, did you hear that there were a number of units calling themselves the Red Berets in the same area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, around the time we are discussing, that is to say, in April and May 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. One of them was more than enough for me. I don't know whether there were any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of the Micas or Preda's Wolves. They came from the Doboj region, which isn't too far.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about the Micas later and their crimes in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Next, I'd like to go to a portion of your statement having to do with the attack on the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is page 7, the same document, P173. In the B/C/S, it's page 7, and page 6 in the English version, in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It says: "The town center was being protected by 50 men." My first question: Who were these 50 men protecting the town center?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I still don't have the document before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Document P173, page 6 in English, and 7 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, the second paragraph on the left-hand side of the screen, can you see it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who were these 50 men?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Locals. Mostly Muslims, I think, from the TO, from the SDA, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The next sentence. I suppose those people were armed?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so as well. I didn't see them, but I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The next sentence: "Arkan first attacked the police station, but couldn't get to the center." My first question concerning this sentence is: It seems that Arkan tried to attack the police station, but failed to occupy it; did I understand this sentence correctly?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. First of all, Arkan, in this context, refers to the special forces, and he did take the police station, but didn't dare or couldn't go further towards the center because the other groups appeared. That's what I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So when you, in your statements, say "Arkan," or "the Red Berets," or "the Grey Wolves," you actually mean the specials?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What about the word "Arkan;" how did that get into this sentence?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who made the transcript and how it was formulated. Well, it was probably written the way I said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I put it to you that Arkan and what is usually referred to as Arkan's group were not in Bosanski Samac at all concerning the events that you described.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Arkan, himself, but his men or parts of his unit were there, because they showed their insignia to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Further down the paragraph, it says: "Arkan's and Seselj's men were already killing people in the town." Where did you get this information, that Arkan's and Seselj's men were killing people around town?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Misa Pavlovic's house, who was my neighbour, and there was a phone call. They said that a Croat was killed in Donja Mahala by Seselj's men. That's the information we had. And that's how I conveyed it. Ordinary people didn't know who was who. It was a word of mouth, and that's how I described it in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, I wanted to ask you something about an event which I'm pretty sure you are familiar with. Did you hear that in Pelagicevo there were 25 people who were taken out of a bus and taken to the police station in Samac; some of them were later taken to Crkvine, and some of them were killed there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that group which may have been brought in from Pelagicevo, but I do know that a group of people was killed in Crkvine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: They were stopped in Pelagicevo and taken off the bus.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you properly, you know of the event in Crkvine?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to show you a document, which is D10. It's a document by the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, signed by Mr. Amir Ahmic, Office for Co-operation with this Tribunal. I suppose you're familiar with this decree -- with this document -- with this office?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the document, but I am familiar with the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In item 3 of the document of the Government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, it says: "Srecko Radovanovic, aka Debeli ..." So your government is informing the Tribunal that according to the date available to them, Radovanovic, aka, Debeli, commanded the 2nd Posavina Brigade of the BSA and ordered the arrest of a group of 25 passengers from a bus on the road Brcko-Doboj. This incident took place in Pelagicevo, the area of Bosanska Posavina in the beginning of the war. The arrested were transported to the prison of the public security service in Bosanski Samac and spent, there, a few days in detention. Then they were transferred to the prison in the village of Crkvine, near Bosanski Samac. According to the survivors, there were 18 detainees killed at the camp in Crkvine during the night between the 7th and 8th of May." Does this tally with what you know about the event?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less. I even attended the funeral of the bodies exhumed after the mass grave was found. And then it was said that a number of them were taken off the bus and taken there with other people from Bosanski Samac, where they were killed. I didn't know that they came from Pelagicevo, though. I only remember that mention was made of people taken off the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So your government informed this Tribunal that Srecko Radovanovic, aka Debeli, was responsible for that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the stopping of the bus, that he's responsible for the stopping of the bus?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, we can read it together. It says that he's responsible for the entire incident.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That cannot be true. Someone else is responsible for the incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just -- you're referring that he was held responsible for the whole of it. Where exactly do I find that in this letter, Mr. Petrovic ? I'm just trying to follow your line of thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will try to interpret or explain my understanding. The first sentence says: "Please find below available information about criminal files of the individuals listed here." First we have Abramovic, then Vakic, then Radovanovic, and then Crnic. The way I understand this document is that this entire event is ascribed to the person in item 3. I believe it is clear from the structure of the document, based on the first sentence of the document. That's my understanding. Also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document describes what followed -- what followed after Radovanovic, as commander of the 2nd Posavina Brigade, had ordered the arrest. Now, you can put him responsible for having triggered what happened later. There are several modes of liability. But the document, itself, describes what Mr. Radovanovic did and what then subsequently, by whomever, happened. If that is your interpretation, if you say the document -- if the witness -- you asked the witness -- you say: "Well, we can read it together. It says that he's responsible for the entire incident." Would you please refrain from putting to the witness what is your interpretation of a document, especially if that is an interpretation which is not beyond the realm of dispute. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, may I explain very briefly. I did not wish to go into any detail before this witness. (Redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: (redacted). I do apologise, but I had to explain how come I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
